title: Bone Marrow Sampling: Site, Dry Tap, Leukoerythroblastic Film and Perls Iron
summary: Learn why the posterior iliac crest is the preferred marrow site, what aspirate and core biopsy each show, what a dry tap and a leukoerythroblastic film suggest, and how Perls storage-iron grading works and where its scales differ.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 31 Hits 8 (Perls storage iron), 9 (leukoerythroblastosis), 10 (posterior iliac crest; dry tap needs biopsy) and Exam Trap 6 (dry tap). Site and specimen roles from Ridgeway 2017, Hjortholm 2013 and Bhaskar 2021; dry tap from Bhaskar 2021, Ridgeway 2017 and Chew 2024; leukoerythroblastic picture from Langabeer 2025 and Chew 2024; Perls chemistry from Sonoda 2025; grading from Phiri 2009 (Gale scale) and Lahtiharju 2025. Hit 8 is qualified (register flag rv-perls-grade-scale): the conventional Gale scale runs 0–6, not 0–5+, and grading is not standardised; the reviewer’s “normal adult is 2+” is not taught. Hit 9 is qualified (register flag rv-leukoerythroblastic-causes): reactive causes (haemolysis, haemorrhage, megaloblastic anaemia, infection) also produce the picture. Bain 2001 (J Clin Pathol) was reachable only as an abstract and is not cited. The ICSH bone marrow guideline (Lee 2008) is not open access and was not read.

objectives: State the preferred adult marrow site and the alternatives, and what aspirate and core biopsy each show.
Explain what a dry tap suggests and why it calls for a core biopsy.
Define a leukoerythroblastic blood picture and list infiltrative and reactive causes.
Describe what the Perls stain detects and why storage-iron grades depend on the scale and on adequate fragments.

scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a 64-year-old with anaemia and a large spleen. The blood film shows nucleated red cells and myelocytes. A marrow aspiration from the posterior iliac crest yields no marrow fluid (a “dry tap”). A Perls iron stain is also requested. The marrow aspiration from the back of the hip brings up no marrow fluid at all: a dry tap. An iron stain has also been requested.
What does the film suggest, and what should happen after a dry tap?

scenes.title: Where and what to sample
scenes.altText: Schematic pelvis (not to scale) with three sites. Posterior iliac crest: preferred site for aspiration and trephine biopsy in adults — no major nerves nearby when the correct area is located; chosen for safety and convenience. Anterior iliac crest: used when the posterior crest is inaccessible (immobility, obesity, injury). Sternum: aspirate only, not trephine; risk of cardiac tamponade. Two specimen cards: aspirate smear = cell morphology and differential counts including blasts; spicules in the aspirate show that the marrow cavity was reached. Trephine (core) biopsy = marrow architecture, overall cellularity (haematopoietic tissue vs fat), stroma and fibrosis.

cues.text: In adults, the posterior iliac crest is the preferred site for both aspiration and core biopsy. It is chosen for safety and convenience: there are no major nerves there if the right area is found.

If the back of the hip cannot be reached, because of immobility, obesity or injury, the anterior iliac crest is used. The sternum is suitable for aspirate only, not a core, and carries a risk of cardiac tamponade.

The two specimens answer different questions. The aspirate smear shows individual cell morphology and gives the differential count, including blasts. Small bony spicules in the aspirate show the needle reached the marrow cavity.
The core biopsy keeps the architecture: overall cellularity, the balance of blood-forming tissue and fat, and the stroma, where fibrosis shows.

scenes.title: Leukoerythroblastic film and the dry tap
scenes.altText: Left card: leukoerythroblastic blood picture = myeloid precursors (myelocytes or promyelocytes) plus nucleated red cells in the blood film; often with poikilocytosis and a normocytic anaemia. Causes listed in one review: marrow-infiltrating solid tumours, haematological malignancies (a frequent but not invariable feature of primary and post-PV/post-ET myelofibrosis), but also haemolysis, liver disease, megaloblastic anaemia, haemorrhage and acute infection. Right card: dry tap = failure to obtain marrow fluid. It may be technical (needle position). Repeated dry taps have been linked with myelofibrosis, a marrow packed with leukaemic cells, hairy cell leukaemia, lymphoma, metastatic tumour, aplastic anaemia or Paget disease. Action: core biopsy is needed to find the process; touch imprints of the unfixed core can stand in for aspirate smears.

cues.text: A leukoerythroblastic film has immature myeloid cells, such as myelocytes, together with nucleated red cells in the blood. It often comes with poikilocytosis and a normocytic anaemia.

Marrow infiltration is a major cause: metastatic solid tumours, blood cancers, and myelofibrosis, where it is frequent but not invariable. But the same picture also follows haemolysis, haemorrhage, megaloblastic anaemia, liver disease and acute infection.

A dry tap means no marrow fluid comes up. Sometimes the needle is simply in the wrong place. Repeated dry taps can point to marrow disease: myelofibrosis, a marrow packed with leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, lymphoma, metastatic tumour, or even aplastic anaemia.
So a persistent dry tap is not solved by more aspirating. A core biopsy is needed to show the process, and touch imprints of the fresh core can replace the missing aspirate smears.

scenes.title: Reading a Perls iron stain
scenes.altText: Perls card: acid releases ferric iron from haemosiderin, which reacts with potassium ferrocyanide to form blue Prussian blue. Haem iron (haemoglobin) is not released by the acid, so it does not stain. Grading card (Gale scale as tabulated in Phiri 2009): grade 0 none … grade 6 very heavy; grades 0–1 counted as deficient storage iron in that study; fragment grade 2 or more counted as iron present; fragments must be adequate (that study graded only smears with at least seven fragments). Scale card: grading is subjective and not standardised; a large 2025 study reported iron simply as none, low, normal or abundant. Hook answers: (1) film: leukoerythroblastic, consider infiltration or myelofibrosis but also reactive causes; (2) dry tap: core biopsy with touch imprints; (3) a Perls grade needs fragment-rich aspirate, so it may come from the imprints or not at all.

cues.text: The Perls stain uses acid to free ferric iron from haemosiderin, the storage iron, and ferrocyanide turns it Prussian blue. Haem iron inside haemoglobin is not freed by the acid, so haemoglobin itself stays unstained.

Storage iron is graded in marrow fragments. On the conventional Gale scale, grades run from zero, none, to six, very heavy. In one study, grade zero or one counted as deficient stores, and smears without enough fragments were not graded.
Scales are not standardised and grading is subjective. A large 2025 study simply reported none, low, normal or abundant. So check which scale a report uses.
Back to the hook. The film is leukoerythroblastic: think infiltration or fibrosis, but rule out reactive causes. The dry tap needs a core biopsy, and an iron grade needs a fragment-rich specimen.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A dry tap means repeat the aspirate until it works” (✓ after checking needle position, a persistent dry tap needs a core biopsy; suspect fibrosis or a packed marrow); “Myelocytes plus nucleated red cells always mean tumour in the marrow” (✓ infiltration is a major cause, but haemolysis, haemorrhage, megaloblastic anaemia and infection also produce it); “Perls stains all the iron in the marrow, including haemoglobin” (✓ only non-haem storage iron, mainly haemosiderin).

cues.text: Trap one: a dry tap means keep aspirating. No: once needle position is checked, a persistent dry tap calls for a core biopsy to find the cause, such as fibrosis or a packed marrow.
Trap two: a leukoerythroblastic film always means tumour. No: infiltration is a major cause, but haemolysis, bleeding, megaloblastic anaemia and infection can do it too.
Trap three: Perls stains all the iron. No: it shows non-haem storage iron, mainly haemosiderin. Haemoglobin iron stays unstained.

props.title: ✗ “Dry tap: just aspirate again.”
lines: ✓ Core biopsy; suspect fibrosis or packing

scenes.title: Back door, dry well, blue vault
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Enter by the BACK DOOR (posterior iliac crest). If the WELL is DRY, dig a CORE instead of pumping harder. Then open the BLUE VAULT (Perls) to count the stored iron.” Tokens: back door = posterior crest · dry well = core biopsy · blue vault = storage iron. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: enter by the back door, the posterior iliac crest. If the well is dry, dig a core instead of pumping harder. Then open the blue vault, the Perls stain, to see the stored iron.

Where it breaks: a dry tap can be just a misplaced needle; the vault grade depends on the scale and on enough fragments; and a leukoerythroblastic film is not proof of anything in the vault or the well.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Posterior iliac crest · dry tap → core biopsy + imprints”, “Leukoerythroblastic film: infiltration or reactive · Perls = storage iron, scale-dependent”.

cues.text: Sample the marrow from the posterior iliac crest, answer a persistent dry tap with a core biopsy, treat a leukoerythroblastic film as a reason to look for marrow infiltration while remembering reactive causes, and grade Perls storage iron only on adequate fragments with the lab’s own scale.

Leukoerythroblastic: infiltration or reactive · Perls = storage iron

explanation.what: Plain language: a marrow sample is usually taken from the back of the hip bone. Liquid marrow (aspirate) shows the cells one by one; a solid core shows how the marrow is built. If no liquid comes out, the marrow may be scarred or crammed, so a core is taken. Immature white cells and nucleated red cells in the blood can mean the marrow is being crowded out, but stress states cause it too. A blue iron stain shows the iron stored in the marrow. Scientific terms: posterior iliac crest, aspirate, spicules, trephine (core) biopsy, touch imprint, dry tap, myelofibrosis, leukoerythroblastic blood picture, Perls (Prussian blue) reaction, haemosiderin, Gale grading.
explanation.why: Choosing the safest site with good marrow, knowing which specimen answers which question, and recognising when an aspirate cannot be obtained prevents repeated futile procedures and missed fibrosis or infiltration. Storage iron in the marrow is a long-standing reference for iron deficiency, but its grading is subjective.
explanation.measure: Site: posterior iliac crest preferred in adults; anterior crest if inaccessible; sternum aspirate only. Aspirate adequacy: spicules visible. Dry tap: check needle position; persistent dry tap → core biopsy, with touch imprints in place of smears. Perls: acid releases ferric iron from haemosiderin, ferrocyanide forms Prussian blue; haem iron not stained. Gale scale 0 (none) to 6 (very heavy); in Phiri 2009 grades 0–1 = deficient stores and only smears with at least 7 fragments were graded.
explanation.differs: Aspirate (cells, counts) vs core (architecture, cellularity, fibrosis); technical dry tap vs pathological dry tap; infiltrative vs reactive leukoerythroblastic picture; haemosiderin (stains) vs haem iron (does not).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next step after a dry tap, the preferred marrow site, what a leukoerythroblastic film suggests, or what the Perls stain detects. If an item quotes a 0–5+ scale, apply the scale given in the item.

questions.stem: Repeated attempts at marrow aspiration from the posterior iliac crest yield no marrow fluid despite correct needle position. What is the best next step?

options.text: Obtain a core (trephine) biopsy and make touch imprints
options.rationale: Correct. A biopsy is needed after a dry tap to show the underlying process, such as fibrosis or a packed marrow, and touch imprints of the core can replace the smears.

options.text: Keep aspirating at the same site until fluid returns
options.rationale: Incorrect. Once needle position is correct, more aspiration attempts leave the cause unknown; a core biopsy is what shows it.
Incorrect. No marrow was examined, so cellularity is unknown; dry taps occur with packed marrows (leukaemia, lymphoma, tumour) and fibrosis as well as aplastic anaemia, and the core shows which.

options.text: Switch to a sternal core biopsy
options.rationale: Incorrect. The sternum is suitable for aspirate only, not trephine biopsy, and carries a tamponade risk.

questions.stem: A blood film shows myelocytes and nucleated red cells. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It is a leukoerythroblastic picture; marrow infiltration is a major cause, but reactive causes such as haemolysis or haemorrhage must be considered
options.rationale: Correct. Infiltration and myelofibrosis are important causes, but haemolysis, haemorrhage, megaloblastic anaemia and infection also produce it.

options.text: It proves metastatic carcinoma in the marrow
options.rationale: Incorrect. The picture is not specific; reactive causes also produce it.

options.text: It is a normal finding in adults
options.rationale: Incorrect. Nucleated red cells and myelocytes are not expected in adult blood.

options.text: It is always seen in myelofibrosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is frequent but not invariable in myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: What does the Perls (Prussian blue) stain detect in a marrow aspirate?

options.rationale: Correct. Acid releases ferric iron from haemosiderin, which forms Prussian blue with ferrocyanide.
Incorrect. Haem iron is not released by the acid, so it does not stain.
Incorrect. Serum ferritin is measured by immunoassay, not by staining a smear.
Incorrect. This is a serum calculation from iron and transferrin.

claims.text: Posterior iliac crest preferred in adults; anterior crest alternative; sternum aspirate only with tamponade risk.
Aspirate shows morphology and counts; spicules confirm cavity reached; core shows architecture, cellularity, stroma.
Dry tap: may be technical; repeated dry taps linked with fibrosis, packed marrow, aplastic anaemia and other disease; core biopsy needed; touch imprints replace smears.
Leukoerythroblastic picture definition and infiltrative plus reactive causes; frequent but not invariable in myelofibrosis.
Perls detects haemosiderin non-haem iron; haem iron does not stain.
Serum ferritin is measured by immunoassay and transferrin saturation is calculated from iron and transferrin (question distractors).
Gale scale 0–6; grades 0–1 deficient in one study; adequate fragments needed; grading subjective and not standardised.
Reviewer’s 0–5+ scale with “normal adult is 2+” and “5+ = hemochromatosis/transfusion” memory hook; reported 4–7% dry tap incidence.
claims.note: No open source read gives a 0–5+ scale with 2+ as normal; not taught. The dry tap incidence appears in Bhaskar 2021 citing older sources not read; not taught.

claims.text: Scenario invented; pelvis and stain drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 31 Hit 8 grades marrow storage iron 0–5+ with normal adult 2+. The conventional Gale scale (as tabulated in Phiri 2009) runs 0–6, Phiri 2009 treats grades 0–1 as deficient and ≥2 as iron present, and Lahtiharju 2025 notes there is no standardised interpretation method; Hit 8 also says the stain shows ferritin, but Sonoda 2025 states ferritin iron is too scarce to detect. The lesson teaches that grades depend on the scale (register flag rv-perls-grade-scale).

Ch. 31 Hit 9 links leukoerythroblastosis to marrow space occupation. Langabeer 2025 lists infiltrative causes but also haemolysis, liver disease, megaloblastic anaemia, haemorrhage and acute infection; the lesson teaches both (register flag rv-leukoerythroblastic-causes).
